catalog_quote: As regards Accent, the general rule is to throw it back as far as possible, but there are exceptions, and in such case the accent will be indicated by a ′ on the accented vowel, as in dekhᵃláhᵘ̃ quoted above. The accent cannot be thrown further back than the antepenultimate, and if the penultimate is long the accent falls on it. Thus, dekhalᵃkaínhⁱ, not dekhalákainhⁱ. / Rule of the Short Antepenultimate. / The following rule, known as the Rule of the Short Antepenultimate, is most important. It runs through the whole Bihārī language ... It should be remembered that it only applies to Tadbhava words. ... d. In counting syllables for the above rules, ऐ ai and औ au, as already stated, count as two, thus, देखै dekhai, he sees. The imperfect vowels इ i and उ u, at the end of a word, are not counted as syllables, nor is the silent अ a in the same position.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (archive.org;ernet.dli.2015.107134, 482 pp., text layer present) plus its scanned twin line 4335 ff.). I rendered PDF page 44 (printed p. 24, running header 'BIHĀRĪ.', within the section whose facing rectos are headed 'INTRODUCTION, MAITHILĪ' pp. 21, 23) and read the page image. The passage is there word for word: 'As regards Accent, the general rule is to throw it back as far as possible, but there are exceptions, and in such case the accent will be indicated by a ′ on the accented vowel, as in dekhᵃlā́hᵘ̃ quoted above. The accent cannot be thrown further back than the antepenultimate, and if the penultimate is long the accent falls on it. Thus, dekhalᵃkaínhⁱ, not dekhalákain…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is retracted as far from the end of the word as possible, but no further than the antepenultimate syllable; a long (heavy) penult attracts the accent; otherwise (light penult) the antepenult is accented. Lexical exceptions exist and are marked with an acute in Grierson's transcription. (Final silent -a and the 'imperfect' final i/u are not counted as syllables, per the adjacent Rule of the Short Antepenultimate.)
new_statements.exceptions: 'there are exceptions', marked ad hoc with an acute accent on the accented vowel (e.g. dekhᵃlắhũ); no list given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent, stated for Maithilī (Grierson's Maithilī explicitly includes the Chhikā-chhikī bolī of Bhagalpur/Monghyr/Santal Parganas = Angika); the section immediately precedes the 'Rule of the Short Antepenultimate' said to run 'through the whole Bihārī language'.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand accent statement found is Grierson's (LSI V.2, 1903) rule for Maithilī as a whole (mait1250-level 'Bihārī/Maithilī' introduction, pronunciation section). Grierson classifies Angika as the 'Chhikā-chhikī bolī' sub-dialect of Maithilī (South Bhagalpur, east South Monghyr, N/W Santal Parganas; LSI V.2 pp. 95-96) and says its grammar 'closely resembles' the Maithili of Madhipura/Purnea, so the rule is intended to cover it, but it is not stated for Angika separately. No modern Angika-specific (angi1238) phonological description mentioning stress could be located or opened.

readall_conflicts: The only tension on record is second-hand: Yadav 1984 (pp. Yadav's own instrumental findings for Maithili (his section 5.3) are not part of this angi1238 record. Between Jha (as reported) and the catalog's Grierson 1903 statement the type agrees (weight-sensitive, three-syllable window) but the default in the absence of long vowels differs in wording (Grierson: thrown back as far as possible; Jha: penult).
